title: AI Leaders Are Refineries, Not Winners of Native Apps
dek: AI enters the agent era: first-phase leaders are just refineries, not winners of native apps; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organizations shift from roles to tasks; ultimately, humans compete on the ability to create something from nothing.
why: Zeng Ming offers a three-phase industrial history framework to help you locate AI's current position, countering the 'this time is different' optimism, while also revealing the opportunity window for application entrepreneurs and the brutal expectations for giants' transformation.
who: CEOs making AI strategy, executives at traditional giants seeking a second curve, AI investors, and tech founders torn between building models or applications.
skip: The quick Q&A and book list at the end can be skipped (after 2:29).

points.h: Building agents today is like building websites in 1992
points.body: Zeng Ming divides the industrialization of general-purpose technologies into three phases: first becoming social infrastructure, then an explosion of applications, and finally native applications. The consensus on token as a unit of measure by 2026 signals the maturity of the first phase; the agent events around Chinese New Year (colloquially 'lobster') mark AI's official entry into the agent era. He compares this to the website-building movement of 1992: then people built websites to share information; today they build agents to share capabilities. The browser hasn't appeared yet; those who can establish agent standards and capture user entry points may hold the biggest opportunity in the next two years.

points.h: A ten-trillion-dollar company will emerge, but not these two
points.body: Zeng Ming states plainly that OpenAI and Anthropic are remarkable technical and commercial achievements, but business history shows that the first wave of companies is unlikely to be the big winners of the native application phase. Yahoo was worth $120 billion five years after founding, and AOL reached a $220 billion valuation, yet neither became the Google of the next era. Model companies are more like AI cloud companies or refineries that extract base oil; the real application value belongs to chemical plants and car companies—and cars weren't built by oil companies. He believes a ten-trillion-dollar company will surely emerge, but it may not be the current leaders. Model companies will evolve into mature businesses characterized by oligopoly and heavy government regulation.

points.h: The unit of AI-native organizations is tasks, not roles
points.body: Companies correspond to the industrial-era bureaucracy; AI disrupts the industrial era, so the corporate system will decline. The basic unit of an AI-native organization is not a role but a task: people organize not by reporting lines but by 'what problem needs solving,' with both humans and AI collaborating around tasks. Thus, well-designed jobs and hierarchies will disappear, and traditional middle management will die out. Future founders must first define their organization's task network. Silicon Valley's NewLab is a prototype of this new organizational form; OpenAI itself resembles a lab more than a traditional company. The culture of new organizations is more like a sports team, emphasizing transparency, sharing, and co-creation, rather than command and assessment.

points.h: Excellence is judged only in hindsight; being good is visible on the spot
points.body: Zeng Ming argues that 'excellent is not the same as great.' Excellence is growth sustained by positive feedback, while greatness requires overcoming repeated negative feedback, persisting when everyone disagrees, and ultimately proving oneself a prophet of the era through enormous success—so 'greatness is determined after the fact.' Those who are merely excellent often fall into a cycle of proving themselves, leading to conservative strategies. Truly great people have a small ego, attribute success to the times and their partners, and are driven by mission rather than external valuation. When identifying founders, he asks, 'What kind of self would you be satisfied with in ten years?' If the answer is 'a company worth ten billion dollars,' that's primarily ego-driven, not an intrinsic mission. Truly great founders are often altruistic and empathetic.

points.h: Strategy in the AI era cannot be planned; it must be generated
points.body: In the AI era, strategy is not planning but generation. Zeng Ming proposes a 'strategy generation system': organizations must build an environment and network that allows strategic insights to emerge naturally. Because decision frequency is higher and quality demands are greater, CEOs cannot rely on linear extrapolation for planning, nor can they outsource strategy to McKinsey—McKinsey's rise was a product of the slow maturation of the industrial era. His methodology is 'look ten years, think three years, act one year,' with the core being 'think three years': you must see at least two or three milestones ahead, creating tension between short-term actions and the medium-term vision. Organizational design must ensure sufficient context rather than control, enabling the right people to make the right decisions at the right time.

points.h: The correct analogy for robots is appliances, not cars
points.body: Zeng Ming believes robots are still in the strategic exploration phase, far from convergence. Currently, two paths—building a generalized brain first or achieving closed-loop scenarios first—are both logically valid, and it's impossible to judge which will be faster. Historically, the auto industry had thousands of companies from 1900 to 1920, until Ford's assembly line in 1913 brought scale; robots haven't yet had their Model T moment, and selling ten thousand units would already be remarkable. But a better analogy for robots is appliances rather than cars: after electricity, refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners, and countless other categories emerged. Robots interacting with the physical world will have N major scenarios, and home, companionship, and industrial uses may each produce their own native giants.

points.h: Giants that feel safe are the most unsafe
points.body: Zeng Ming says that in the face of a tidal wave, no one is safe; feeling safe is the most unsafe. In business history, no company has ever smoothly transitioned from one era to the next. IBM and Microsoft are the only possible exceptions, and both are fraught with uncertainty. AI is a productivity revolution that disrupts the industrial revolution, not a continuation innovation like mobile internet, so the technological reserves and organizational culture of old giants are liabilities. Google can survive as an AI cloud company but may not capture the consumer entry point; ByteDance has an AI cloud opportunity, but Doubao is not the future application; Tencent's social relationships will be restructured; Alibaba is not naturally safe either. New platforms will likely be created by new companies.

points.h: Human value lies in creating from nothing, not in writing songs or painting
points.body: Drawing on Drucker's framework, Zeng Ming defines the AI era as the age of creativity: all knowledge work that can be structured will be taken over by AI. Humans are both forced and finally liberated to develop new potential. This potential is creativity—not writing songs or painting, but the ability to originally define complex problems and create something from nothing. AI has already taken all existing knowledge; human value lies in creating what does not yet exist. He therefore calls his mission 'being a happy researcher' and believes civilization's next step will reorganize around creativity. Even the education system will be forced to shift from 'knowledge indoctrination' to 'open exploration,' because young people already know the old path leads nowhere.

terms.def: Treating AI compute as infrastructure that produces tokens, symbolizing intelligence entering a standardized, metered phase.
An operating system that can directly orchestrate all agents to complete tasks based on intent; Zeng Ming believes this belongs to the third phase and cannot be implemented yet.
A new organizational form dissatisfied with the corporate model, composed mainly of researchers; OpenAI is seen as the earliest example.
A Silicon Valley buzzword meaning taking control of one's own destiny, proactively seeking tasks and growth, replacing hierarchical command.
A management philosophy: provide ample shared context and information, allowing members to make correct decisions autonomously.

quotes.text: The most successful companies must be contrarian, but being contrarian doesn't guarantee success.
It may not survive to the end. It will likely do well for a while, but it probably won't be the big player, the big winner in the native application phase.
Companies from the first phase struggle to survive into the second, and those from the second struggle into the third.

So companies will disappear; companies will die out. There's nothing to regret about that. In the future, there will be more interesting things. How many people today are happy going to work at a company? They're not.

My technology is so great, I've created so much value, why might my company not be worth much? Because of a basic economic law: as long as there is homogeneous supply, you cannot capture high profits. You're just a company that isn't worth much.

Greatness is determined after the fact, because you overcome negative feedback again and again. When everyone doesn't recognize you, you finally prove through enormous success that you were the earliest prophet of the era.
I've always believed that in the face of a tidal wave, no one is safe. Whoever feels safe is the most unsafe.
